raw_case_text:
The patient was a 59-year-old male from Dammam, Saudi Arabia with a history of HIV for 15 years, who was non-compliant to HIV treatment for five years. The patient last visited the HIV clinic in December 2020 and blood tests showed a viral load of 9340 copies per mL. Furthermore, this person had a history of HBV (immune to hepatitis B due to natural immunity), chronic non-treated HCV, diabetes mellitus type II for three years, hypertension (HTN), smoking and active drug abuse for heroin and alcohol, chronic kidney disease stage III, and a previously treated cervical spine abscess with internal fixation surgery. The patient was prescribed tenofovir and emtricitabine; no antiretroviral resistance screening test was performed, and we could not obtain lymphocyte subset results. Prior to emergency department (ER) admittance, the patient had three months history of progressive neck pain, and sudden weakness in the upper and lower limbs the day before presenting to the ER; however, they experienced no numbness, loss of sphincter control, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. The results of the patient's physical examination, blood pressure and other vital signs were normal, and neuromuscular examination results were unremarkable. However, laboratory blood test results revealed a high white blood cell (WBC) count, decreased hemoglobin level (Hgb), and high platelet count (Plt). The patient's serum creatinine level was 2.54 mg/dL and blood urea nitrogen was 45 mg/dL. Notably, there were elevated levels of inflammatory markers, such as procalcitonin and C-reactive protein, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate. A brain computed tomography (CT) revealed chronic small vessel disease, with a number of lytic lesions on the patient's first cervical vertebra.
Seven days post admission, the patient experienced fever (38.8 C), in addition to persistent and uncontrolled high blood pressure; however, a physical examination showed no evidence of limited movement or mobility. Prior to receiving blood culture results for sepsis testing, vancomycin and meropenem antibiotics were empirically prescribed. The patient received a complete work-up, and was tested for complete blood count (CBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), procalcitonin, and blood and urine cultures.
The septic workup results showed a high WBC count and high levels of inflammatory markers, including CRP and procalcitonin (Table 1). 
We incubated one set of blood culture vials in a BacT/Alert Virtuo system (BioMerieux, France) for 5 days, according to the internal policies and procedures of the microbiology laboratory at King Fahd Hospital of the University. After 72 hours of incubation, one of the two blood culture vials flagged positive, and direct Gram staining showed Gram-positive bacilli. Subsequently, the blood culture vials were sub-cultured on sheep blood, MacConkey, chocolate, and anaerobic Brucella agars.
After 48 hours incubation at 37 C, there was no growth present on sheep blood, MacConkey's, and chocolate agars. However, there was bacterial growth on anaerobic Brucella agar (Figure 1). We used Matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization-time of flight-mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF-MS) (VITEK MS; bioMerieux) and the Knowledge Base database (version 3.0) with a confidence value of 99.9% to identify Clostridium paraputrificum. Antibiotics-susceptibility tests for anaerobic organisms were not available in our routine diagnostic laboratory; therefore, we depended on 2022 Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) cumulative data, which showed that Clostridium was sensitive to imipenem, meropenem, and metronidazole antibiotics. Urine analysis results were normal, and the urine culture showed no growth. 
Forty-eight hours following treatment with vancomycin and meropenem antibiotics, the patient clinically improved, the fever subsided, and blood cultures showed no growth. All subsequent cultures were negative, but inflammatory markers remained high. On day 12 of admission, the patient experienced sudden cardiac arrest due to reflex arrhythmia caused by atlantoaxial subluxation and passed away.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 59-year-old male from Dammam, Saudi Arabia, presented to the emergency department with a 3-month history of progressive neck pain and a 1-day history of sudden-onset upper and lower limb weakness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed progressive neck pain over the 3 months prior to presentation, followed by acute onset of weakness involving both the upper and lower extremities the day before emergency department admission.
subjective.past_medical_history: History of HIV infection for 15 years with non-compliance to antiretroviral therapy for 5 years (last HIV clinic visit in December 2020 showed a viral load of 9,340 copies/mL; lymphocyte subset results were unavailable and no antiretroviral resistance screening was performed). Past history also includes resolved hepatitis B virus infection (natural immunity), chronic untreated hepatitis C virus infection, type 2 diabetes mellitus for 3 years, hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage III, previously treated cervical spine abscess with internal fixation surgery, smoking, and active heroin and alcohol abuse.
subjective.review_of_systems: Negative for numbness, loss of sphincter control, fever, night sweats, or weight loss prior to presentation. Prescribed home medications included tenofovir and emtricitabine (non-compliant).

objective.physical_examination: Initial vital signs including blood pressure were normal, and physical and neuromuscular examinations were unremarkable. On hospital day 7, the patient developed fever (38.8 °C) and persistent uncontrolled hypertension without limited movement or mobility.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial blood tests showed elevated WBC count, decreased hemoglobin, elevated platelet count, serum creatinine 2.54 mg/dL, BUN 45 mg/dL, and elevated procalcitonin, CRP, and ESR. Urinalysis was normal. Repeat septic workup on day 7 showed persistently elevated WBC count, CRP, and procalcitonin.
objective.advanced_workup: Brain CT demonstrated chronic small vessel disease and multiple lytic lesions involving the first cervical vertebra (C1).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: 59-year-old male with longstanding poorly controlled HIV infection (prior HIV-1 viral load 9,340 copies/mL) complicated by C1 lytic vertebral lesions and healthcare-associated sepsis caused by Clostridium paraputrificum bacteremia. One of two blood culture vials incubated in the BacT/Alert Virtuo system flagged positive at 72 hours with Gram-positive bacilli; subculture grew strictly anaerobic colonies on Brucella agar at 48 hours, identified by MALDI-TOF MS (VITEK MS, 99.9% confidence) as Clostridium paraputrificum (sensitive per CLSI cumulative data to imipenem, meropenem, and metronidazole). Urine culture showed no growth. Empiric intravenous vancomycin and meropenem were initiated on day 7, resulting in defervescence, clinical improvement, and clearance of subsequent blood cultures within 48 hours, though inflammatory markers remained elevated. On hospital day 12, the patient suffered sudden cardiac arrest secondary to reflex arrhythmia from atlantoaxial subluxation and passed away.
